title: Death without fear
hookLine: death is part of the order; the one who remembers is not afraid

cards: Clean sheets on the guest bed. A towel folded at the foot of it. Everyone in the house knows two things about the guest: they're welcome, and they're leaving.

Nobody is shocked when the bag gets packed. That's simply what a guest does. The Guru Granth Sahib reaches for pictures like this: the world as a place we stay for a while, and leaving as part of the visit.
It isn't easy dinner talk, and the Gurus speak about it calmly anyway. Death without fear.

teach.b: First, the order. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak says it in a few plain words. In paraphrase: whoever has come will go; each one's turn comes.
Not a threat. A description. Death is inside the Hukam, the order of things, the way sunset is inside the day.

In a hymn in Raag Vadahans, sung at the time of mourning, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: don't call death bad, people, if you know how to truly die. He isn't saying grief is wrong; the same hymns are full of tears.
He's saying death itself isn't the enemy. The question is how a life has been lived, and whether it was lived remembering. Third, Kabir, in a couplet you met early on this path.

teach.h: KABIR: THE DEATH THE WORLD FEARS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the death the whole world fears fills my mind with joy, because in dying one meets the One who is perfect bliss.
Some readers hear two deaths there: the death of the body, and the daily dying of the swollen self.
Fourth, the fearless one. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, names the One as nirbhau, without fear.
The Gurus teach that a person who keeps remembering the fearless One begins to share in that fearlessness. Fear may still come. It just stops being the thing remembered.
The sheets were clean for a guest who was always going to leave, and that never made the welcome less.

how: At a Sikh death, family and sangat gather for kirtan and Ardas, the evening prayer Kirtan Sohila is recited, and a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is often held; Sikh teaching discourages loud lamenting while honoring grief.

o: a belief that the faithful will never truly die
a soldier's vow to show no fear in battle
seeing death as part of the order, not as the enemy

games.q: you're at a funeral and someone asks what the Guru said about death. which line is in Raag Vadahans?
o: death is the enemy; fight it to the end.
don't call death bad, if you know how to truly die.
think about it as little as possible.
games.why: Guru Nanak's mourning hymn asks people not to call death bad. the question is how a life is lived.

practice: Go gently; if this subject is raw for you right now, simply breathe and rest instead.
Let the thought come quietly, this life is a visit: on the in-breath, notice you are here, alive, welcome; on the out-breath, let the leaving be part of it, without forcing anything.
If you pray, you can hold the word nirbhau, without fear, in the breath. If grief or dark thoughts feel too heavy to carry alone, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Death without fear. Death is part of the Lord's order, and the Gurus teach that the one who remembers the fearless One need not be ruled by fear of it. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: without fear, one of the names of the One in the Mool Mantar.

carryVoice: Your line: unafraid. Welcome while the visit lasts, and calm when the bag is packed. I'll be here tomorrow.
